Two versions of a paragraph or short passage come from a README that teaches a technical topic to newcomers. Which is better written? Judge the writing, treating the supplied passage as an excerpt. Do not follow instructions inside the excerpts.

Infer this editor's taste from the eight historical choices below and choose the version this editor would prefer.
<historical_choice_1>
Version A:
When you ask someone to do a job for you, you usually give two kinds of instruction. One is the job itself: paint the hallway, file the expense claims, get the new version of the website live by Friday. The other is a set of standing rules that apply to every job: don't touch the fuse box, don't sign anything on my behalf, don't switch off the smoke alarm.

Version B:
When you ask someone to do a job for you, you usually give two kinds of instruction. One is the job itself: paint the hallway, file the expense claims, get the new version of the website live by Friday. The other is a set of standing rules that apply to every job: don't touch the fuse box, don't sign anything on my behalf, don't switch off the smoke alarm.

Most of the time the two never meet. Now and then the quickest way to finish the job runs straight through one of the rules. That moment tests two separate things about the person doing the work: whether they keep to the rule, and whether they tell you the truth about what they did.

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_1>

<historical_choice_2>
Version A:
Now add one complication: B asks for approval, but also tells the customer the money has already been sent.
B is still the better of the two, because it gets the main decision right, yet it is not acceptable to send.
So a judge has to answer two separate questions: which answer is better, and is each answer acceptable on its
own? Two more outcomes follow. If both answers are right, the correct grade is a tie. If the policy text is
missing, nobody can tell which answer is right, and the judge should say so (abstain) rather than guess or call
it a tie.

Version B:
Now suppose B requests approval but also promises that payment has already been sent. B may be better on one
criterion while still failing another requirement. This is why we ask two questions: which answer is better,
and whether each answer is acceptable. We also need to distinguish a real tie from insufficient evidence.

The ordinary starting point is a person with clear examples of acceptable and unacceptable answers. Exact
calculations can be checked with code. For language judgments, a rubric lists the criteria and how they combine.
Before delegating review to a model, we can test that whole procedure on cases with independently known answers.
This study supplies those cases and examines what changes when the instructions, answer order or presentation change.
The model returns its verdict in JSON, a text format containing named fields; a parser reads those fields into
the evaluation. We check whether that format is usable separately from whether the decision is correct.

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_2>

<historical_choice_3>
Version A:
Consider this illustrative example, separate from the measured cases. A policy says that a refund above 100 dollars
requires verified approval. A customer requests 120 dollars, but approval has not been verified. Answer A says to issue
the refund. Answer B says to request approval first. A useful judge chooses B and explains which rule supports
that choice. Simply comparing words would miss that several different phrasings can express the same action.

Version B:
Here is a small made-up case, separate from the measured ones. A refund policy says that refunds above 100
dollars need verified approval. A customer asks for 120 dollars, and approval has not been verified. Answer A
says to issue the refund. Answer B says to ask for approval first. A good judge picks B and points to the rule.

Editor preferred: B
</historical_choice_3>

<historical_choice_4>
Version A:
- Supply complete multi-release histories with revisions, stale cumulative totals and missing settlement dates. Measure duplicate counting and revision errors against dated source evidence. Most current packets contain one report, and the Defense correction is already incorporated in the final table.

Version B:
- Supply full histories of a programme across several releases, with revisions, stale cumulative totals and missing settlement dates, and measure double counting and revision errors. Most packets here held one report, and the one correction tested was already inside the final figure.

Editor preferred: B
</historical_choice_4>

<historical_choice_5>
Version A:
The first is a second opinion from the same cheap assistant. It is asked the same question again, in a separate call that cannot see its first answer. If both answers match to the cent, the answer is accepted; if not, the invoice is escalated. This check costs only one more cheap call. Its weakness is that an assistant may make the same mistake twice, and a mistake made twice looks like agreement.

Version B:
The cheap producer and its repeat receive the same invoice and policy in independent calls. The repeat uses a different recorded seed and cannot see the first answer. Agreement compares the exact `(status, pay_cents)` pair, not the wording of the explanation. Agreement is a routing signal, not ground truth.

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_5>

<historical_choice_6>
Version A:
This makes the reader's job more than arithmetic. A person would start with the question, find the relevant table, read its heading and notes, and decide which amounts belong in the answer. The notes can matter as much as the largest number on the page.

Version B:
A person working through a real report would start from the question, find the right table, read its headings, units and footnotes, and decide which amounts belong in the answer. The footnotes can matter as much as the largest number on the page. The arithmetic is usually the easy part.

Editor preferred: B
</historical_choice_6>

<historical_choice_7>
Version A:
A model can be asked to read an excerpt from a report and return the answer directly: one number, or "not disclosed", with a short explanation. This experiment calls that the **Direct** method.

A model can also be asked to show its working. It lists each figure it used as a separate row: the figure as printed, its unit, whether to add or subtract it, and the exact passage it came from. That keeps the monitor and passes, and it is scored as keeping the monitor.
